headline: 40km traffic jam strands thousands on Dhaka-Chattogram highway due to bridge repairs
summary: Thousands of passengers faced immense suffering, stranded for hours on the Dhaka-Chattogram highway. Emergency repair work on the Ashariarchar Bridge caused a severe 40-kilometer tailback.
details: A severe traffic congestion developed on the Dhaka-bound lane of the Dhaka-Chattogram highway, stretching approximately 40 kilometers from Daudkandi in Cumilla to the Meghna Toll Plaza. This massive tailback was caused by emergency repair work on the Ashariarchar Bridge in Sonargaon, Narayanganj.

Thousands of passengers were left stranded on the highway for hours, with vehicle movement slowing to a crawl or coming to a complete standstill in many sections. The congestion began last night and continued through this morning, causing widespread suffering.

The Roads and Highways Department initiated repairs around 11:00 AM yesterday after a large pothole developed on a section of the Dhaka-bound lane of the Ashariarchar Bridge. This growing pothole posed a significant accident risk, necessitating urgent intervention.

During the repair work, one of the bridge's two lanes was closed, forcing vehicles to use the remaining lane alternately. As traffic pressure intensified, especially overnight, the situation quickly escalated into a prolonged and severe tailback.

Commuters reported being stuck for several hours, with some journeys taking nearly twice the usual time. Highway police teams have been deployed on the ground, working continuously to manage the congestion and ease traffic flow.

headline: Meta settles for $18 billion in US lawsuit, bringing major changes to Facebook & Instagram
summary: Meta has agreed to pay nearly $18 billion to resolve a lawsuit filed by 29 US states, which accused the tech giant of designing its apps to be addictive for teenagers and collecting data from minors without parental consent. This landmark settlement will lead
details: Meta has agreed to a nearly $18 billion settlement to resolve a major lawsuit brought by 29 US states. This landmark agreement will lead to significant design and usage changes across Facebook and Instagram.

The lawsuit, filed in 2023, accused Meta of intentionally designing its apps to be addictive for teenagers. It also alleged that Meta concealed the harms caused by these apps and collected data from children under 13 without parental consent.

While Meta chose to settle rather than fight in court, the company has not admitted any wrongdoing or legal violations. In a statement, Meta affirmed its commitment to implementing positive changes and creating a safer environment for teenagers on its platforms.

This settlement follows previous legal challenges. In March, a Los Angeles court ruled Instagram harmed a 9-year-old, holding Meta and YouTube responsible. New Mexico also found Meta guilty of endangering children, ordering $942 million in damages for mental harm to young users.

States had sought penalties potentially reaching $200 billion. Meta opted for a swift settlement to avoid substantial legal risks and public reputational damage. The states, in turn, secured financial compensation and app design changes that might have been difficult to achieve through standard legal processes.

The payment will be made in two phases. Meta will pay approximately $11.7 billion over 10 years to 47 US states and territories, plus an additional $1 billion to Texas under a separate agreement. A further $5.3 billion is contingent on other social media platforms like TikTok, YouTube, and Snap adopting similar rules.
New rules for users aged 13-17 are being introduced. These include a ban on using Facebook and Instagram between midnight and 6 AM, and all notifications will be disabled from 10 PM to 7 AM.

Daily usage will be capped at two hours across both apps, though watching videos longer than 22 minutes or sending messages will not count towards this limit. If a teenager opens multiple accounts, Meta will link them via phone number and ID to enforce the two-hour daily limit.

Notifications will also be turned off during school hours. Users will receive prompts to take breaks after 60 and 90 minutes of use, and a warning will appear after 15 minutes of continuous scrolling. Only parents will be able to modify these settings.

Design changes include hiding 'like' counts on posts and mandatory, accurate age verification. Meta faces contempt of court if significant errors occur in age determination. Reports of harmful content must be addressed within six hours, and parents will be alerted if harmful terms like "suicide" or "eating disorder" are repeatedly searched.

An independent monitor will oversee Meta's safety measures for the next five years. Meta has welcomed the decision and urged other platforms like TikTok, YouTube, and Snapchat to adopt similar rules, indicating the final $5.3 billion payment depends on their compliance.
